issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: Water/flooding triggers are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another in a car accident, given the rest of the profile centers on crash-related and guilt/shame themes. This trigger introduces a different threat context without support from memory or appraisal items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Feelings' is internally incoherent as worded: 'Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion' describes the opposite of avoidance. Within the maladaptive strategies node, it directly conflicts with an avoidance strategy.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: 'Body Unreliable' fits poorly with the rest of the profile for a perpetration-type accident trauma in which the patient's appraisals otherwise center on guilt, humiliation, and shattered beliefs. There are no memory, trigger, or strategy items suggesting bodily injury, panic/somatic threat, or physical incapacity to support this appraisal.

vignette: Raj was a 42-year-old South Asian man who worked as a tax inspector and had been married for over two decades. His life took an unexpected turn when he accidentally caused a serious injury to another person during a routine traffic stop. The event left him with vivid crash imagery, where scenes of cars hitting each other replayed relentlessly in his mind. He also found himself unable to attend funerals or visit cemeteries without feeling overwhelmed by grief and guilt. Raj had come to believe that he deserved the suffering he was enduring because of what happened, and this belief drove him to suppress thoughts about the trauma whenever possible. The thought, "I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened," often crept into his mind as a form of self-punishment. He also reminded himself that it could have been worse, but this downshifting did little to ease his burden. When Raj recalled the event, he sometimes heard snippets of conversations and sirens in his head, which added to his distress. His memory of the incident was fragmented; some moments were extremely clear while others remained a complete blank. This partial clarity and incomplete picture made him feel like he was only remembering parts of what happened, leaving a sense of incompleteness that haunted him. Raj's negative appraisals compounded his struggles. He felt permanently humiliated by what had occurred, believing that his beliefs about how the world works were completely destroyed. The idea that he should have protected others but failed gnawed at him relentlessly. These feelings of humiliation and shattered beliefs reinforced each other in a vicious cycle, making it difficult for Raj to move forward. The triggers he experienced, such as crash imagery and funerals, often led to his maladaptive strategies of punishing himself and suppressing thoughts about the trauma. The more vividly he remembered parts of the event, the stronger these negative appraisals became. His fragmented memories triggered powerful feelings of humiliation and a sense that he had failed those around him. Over time, Raj's work as a tax inspector became increasingly difficult. He avoided areas with traffic congestion or any situation where there was potential for an accident to occur again. This avoidance affected his ability to conduct thorough inspections and made it challenging to focus on the job at hand. His marriage also began to suffer; he withdrew from family activities, leading to tension and misunderstandings between him and his wife. Raj finally sought help when he realized that his guilt and self-blame were overwhelming both his professional life and personal relationships. He was most afraid of never being able to forgive himself for the accident and feared continuing to live with this profound sense of failure. On the other hand, he hoped that therapy could provide him with a way to process what happened and find some form of peace. In summary, Raj's experience of PTSD was characterized by powerful triggers, maladaptive coping strategies, fragmented memories, and pervasive negative appraisals. His triggers led to self-punishment and thought suppression, while his memory issues reinforced his feelings of humiliation and shattered beliefs. The cycle tightened over time, making it difficult for him to function effectively in both his personal and professional life. His journey to seek help was driven by a deep desire to find a way out of the suffocating grip of guilt and self-blame that had taken hold since the traumatic event.
